question: Oil Record Book Part I records:
options: Cargo tank washing and ballast operations on tankers, recorded by the cargo officer
Ballast water exchange and sediment disposal, as recorded in the ballast water record book
Machinery space operations such as bunkering, sludge disposal and bilge discharge
Garbage disposal and the operation of the incinerator, recorded in Part II of the book
explanation: Entries use the specified codes and item numbers, and each is signed by the officer in charge.

question: Oily bilge water from machinery spaces may be discharged overboard only if its oil content is no more than:
options: 100 ppm
50 ppm
15 ppm
explanation: Discharge must also be via an approved oily water separator with alarm, while en route and outside special areas restrictions.

question: Oil sludge from fuel and lube oil purification should be:
options: Landed to a shore reception facility or burned in an approved incinerator or boiler
Mixed with sewage in the holding tank and discharged together at a safe distance from land
Discharged in special areas only, where the water is deeper than 200 metres
Pumped overboard at night, outside special areas, if the oil content is below 15 ppm
explanation: Sludge tank capacity and disposal must be recorded in the Oil Record Book.

question: Under MARPOL Annex VI, a sealed sample of delivered fuel (MARPOL sample) must be kept:
options: For 7 days after delivery, until the laboratory result for the fuel is received
Permanently, as part of the ship's records, together with the bunker delivery note
For one voyage only, after which the sample is landed at the next port of call
Until the fuel is substantially used, but for at least 12 months from delivery
explanation: The Bunker Delivery Note must be kept on board for three years.

question: NOx Tier III limits apply to marine diesel engines on ships of the relevant build date when they operate:
options: In a NOx Emission Control Area
Only on rivers
Only in port
Anywhere in the world, once the engine has been installed on the ship
explanation: Outside NOx ECAs, Tier II applies. Tier III needs technologies such as SCR or EGR.

question: The EIAPP certificate is issued for:
options: The oily water separator
A marine diesel engine, confirming it meets the NOx limits
The ship's incinerator, confirming that it meets the flue gas limits for dioxins
The ship's sewage plant
explanation: Engine International Air Pollution Prevention certificate. The engine's NOx Technical File must be kept with it.

question: Which of these must NOT be burned in a shipboard incinerator?
options: Paper
Food waste
Oil sludge in an approved incinerator
PCBs and Annex I cargo residues
explanation: Banned items also include garbage with heavy metals and refined products containing halogens. PVC only in type-approved incinerators.

question: An exhaust gas cleaning system (scrubber) is used to:
options: Reduce sulphur oxide emissions so higher-sulphur fuel can be used
Clean ballast water before discharge, by removing the organisms with chemical washwater
Reduce CO2 emissions to zero, by absorbing the gas in the washwater
Treat sewage before discharge, using the washwater circuit of the scrubber plant
explanation: Open-loop scrubbers discharge wash water to sea; some ports and areas restrict this.

question: When changing over to compliant fuel before entering a SOx ECA, the ship must record:
options: Date, time, position and the volume of low-sulphur fuel in each tank
Only the cost of the fuel
Nothing if the changeover is quick
Only the date and time, since the fuel quantities are already shown in the bunker log
explanation: Use a written changeover procedure to make sure compliant fuel is in use before entering the ECA.

question: Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR) reduces NOx by:
options: Injecting urea or ammonia into the exhaust over a catalyst
Burning more fuel in the exhaust manifold to destroy the nitrogen oxides formed
Adding water to the fuel tanks
Recirculating lube oil
explanation: NOx is converted into nitrogen and water vapour.

question: Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) reduces NOx by:
options: Removing sulphur from the fuel before it is injected into the engine cylinders
Raising the combustion temperature, so that nitrogen in the air is burned more completely
Returning some cooled exhaust gas to the intake, which lowers peak combustion temperature
Increasing the oxygen in the cylinder, so that the fuel burns more completely
explanation: Lower peak temperatures reduce thermal NOx formation.

question: IOPP certificate stands for:
options: International Operations and Port Procedures certificate
International Oil Pollution Prevention certificate
Inspection of Oil Purifier Plant certificate
International Onboard Pump Permit
explanation: It is issued under MARPOL Annex I with a supplement (Form A or B) describing the ship's equipment.

question: Bilge holding tanks in the engine room are used to:
options: Store oily bilge water until it can be processed by the OWS or landed ashore
Store fuel for the boiler and the incinerator, to be burned when the ship is in port
Store sewage and grey water until the ship is outside the restricted discharge area
Store fresh water for washing and for use in the engine room workshop
explanation: Holding tanks reduce the need to run the OWS in port or in special areas.

question: The ISPP certificate relates to:
options: Air pollution
Prevention of pollution by sewage
Garbage
Oil pollution, which is dealt with by the IOPP certificate and its supplement
explanation: International Sewage Pollution Prevention certificate, MARPOL Annex IV.

question: Changing the oily water separator's 15 ppm alarm or discharge piping to bypass it is:
options: Allowed if the arrangement is recorded in the log book and removed before arrival in port
Acceptable in open sea, if the officer of the watch is informed first
A serious MARPOL violation that can lead to heavy penalties for the company and crew
Allowed if the chief engineer approves it and the officer of the watch is informed of it
explanation: Unlawful bypassing ('magic pipes') is prosecuted in many countries. Report concerns through the company's procedures.

question: The oily water separator (OWS) is used to:
options: Separate fresh water from sea water in the evaporator, to produce water for the boilers
Treat sewage and grey water from the accommodation before it is discharged overboard
Purify fuel oil for the main engine, removing water and solids before injection
Treat machinery space bilge water so its oil content is 15 ppm or less before discharge
explanation: Separated oil goes to the sludge or bilge oil tank; the clean water passes the oil content meter.

question: The oil content meter of a 15 ppm bilge alarm measures:
options: The engine's fuel consumption
The oil content of the OWS effluent in parts per million
The fuel tank level, which is shown on the sounding gauge in the control room
The salinity of the bilge water
explanation: If the reading exceeds 15 ppm, the alarm sounds and the discharge is stopped or recirculated.

question: The engine room sludge tank collects:
options: Fresh water drained from the boilers and the cooling water system of the engine
Treated sewage from the sewage treatment plant, which is later discharged to the sea
Clean ballast water from the double bottom tanks, ready to be pumped overboard at sea
Oil residues such as purifier sludge, filter drains and drip tray oil
explanation: Sludge is landed ashore or burned in an approved incinerator or boiler.

question: To reduce the risk of an oil spill during bunkering, the ship should:
options: Open the deck scuppers, so that any spill drains overboard and cannot lie on the deck
Fill the tanks to 100% quickly, to reduce the time spent alongside the barge
Use a bunker checklist, keep good communication and monitor tank levels and vents
Leave the manifold unattended once the flow has started, to save manpower on deck
explanation: Drip trays should be in place and SOPEP equipment ready at the manifold.

question: During bunkering, the ship's bunkering operation should be supervised by:
options: The bunker barge crew only, who know the system and the delivery rates of the supplier
Any crew member who is available on deck, with a radio and a copy of the checklist
The cook or steward on duty, who is available on deck while the engineers are at work
A designated responsible officer, usually the chief engineer or an engineer they appoint
explanation: The person in charge agrees the plan, rates and stop signals with the supplier before starting.

question: One good practice to reduce the amount of oily bilge water produced is to:
options: Wash the engine room with large amounts of water every day, and pump it to the bilges
Repair leaks promptly and keep clean water drains separate from oily drains
Leave leaks and drips until the next dry-docking, when all the pipes are repaired together
Pump all clean water, such as cooling water drains, into the bilges to dilute the oil
explanation: Less bilge water means less OWS operation and less waste to land ashore.

question: Using shore power while alongside (cold ironing) mainly helps to:
options: Reduce cargo time
Reduce air emissions from the ship's generators in port
Clean the boiler
Increase the ship's speed in port, by supplying power to the thrusters at all times
explanation: Some ports and regions now require shore power connection for certain ship types.

question: Reducing a ship's speed (slow steaming) lowers her CO2 emissions mainly because:
options: CO2 is not produced at low speed, because the engine then burns only distillate fuel
The engine burns cleaner fuel automatically when the speed is lowered at sea by the bridge
The exhaust gas is filtered by the turbocharger when the engine speed is below half load
Fuel consumption, and therefore CO2 produced, falls sharply at lower speed
explanation: CO2 emissions are directly proportional to the amount of fuel burned.

question: Oily bilge water in the engine room mainly comes from:
options: The cargo holds
Rain water on deck, which drains through the engine room casing into the bilges
Leaks and drains from machinery, pumps, coolers and tanks
Sewage treatment
explanation: Bilge water often contains oil, water, detergents and solid particles.

question: A limit of 15 ppm means:
options: 15 % oil content
15 parts of oil per million parts of the mixture
15 litres of oil per hour, which is the highest rate of discharge permitted
15 grams of oil per litre
explanation: This is equal to about 15 mg of oil per litre of water.

question: MARPOL Annex VI controls sulphur oxide (SOx) emissions mainly by:
options: Banning diesel engines on ships in coastal waters, and allowing only gas turbines to be used
Requiring catalytic converters on all ships, whatever the engine and fuel type fitted
Limiting the engine's speed, so that less fuel is burned in the cylinders
Limiting the sulphur content of fuel oil, or by allowing approved equivalent methods
explanation: The global limit is 0.50% and the ECA limit 0.10%.

question: Entries in Oil Record Book Part I must be:
options: Made only by the shore office, from the readings sent in by the engineer each month
Written only at the end of the voyage, when the engineer has time to write up the operations
Signed by the officer in charge of each operation, and each page by the master
Kept in pencil so they can be changed if the quantities are found to be wrong later
explanation: Entries are in the official language of the flag state and, on international voyages, also English, French or Spanish.

question: Examples of ozone-depleting substances controlled by MARPOL Annex VI include:
options: CFC refrigerants and halon fire-extinguishing agents
Fresh water and steam
Carbon dioxide and nitrogen, which are used in fixed fire-extinguishing systems
Sodium hydroxide
explanation: Deliberate emissions are prohibited, and new installations containing them are banned.

question: NOx is formed in a diesel engine mainly because of:
options: Sulphur in the fuel, which burns to form oxides that combine with the nitrogen
High combustion temperatures causing nitrogen and oxygen in the air to combine
Low cylinder temperatures, which allow nitrogen oxides to form in the unburned fuel
Water in the lubricating oil, which breaks down into oxygen and hydrogen in the cylinder
explanation: This is why NOx reduction methods such as EGR and water injection lower peak combustion temperatures.

question: When sludge or oily bilge water is landed ashore, the ship should obtain and keep:
options: A waste delivery receipt from the reception facility, with the ORB entry
Only a verbal confirmation from the barge master, noted in the engine room log
A copy of the crew list showing the names of those who handled the oily waste
The bunker delivery note for the fuel from which the sludge originated, with its density
explanation: The receipt supports the ORB record during port state and flag inspections.

question: Under MARPOL Annex V, oily rags and used filters from the engine room are treated as:
options: Food waste that may be discharged at sea, more than 12 miles from the nearest land
Sewage, to be treated in the sewage plant before being discharged to the sea
Operational wastes, to be incinerated if permitted or landed ashore
Cargo residues, to be discharged under the same rules as those for the cargo
explanation: They must not be thrown overboard.

question: Among the conditions for discharging processed bilge water from the machinery space outside special areas, the ship must be:
options: Within 3 nautical miles of land, with the OWS in operation and the alarm fitted
In port, with the permission of the agent only, and not in the open sea
Stopped at anchor, with the engines off, to avoid stirring up the sea bed
En route, with the OWS and the 15 ppm alarm and stopping device in operation
explanation: The discharge must not contain chemicals or other substances added to get around the rules.

question: If the oily water separator breaks down, the engineers should:
options: Add detergent to the bilges to break up the oil so that it passes the 15 ppm monitor
Fit a temporary bypass pipe around the separator, so that the bilges can be pumped
Record the failure in the Oil Record Book, keep bilge water on board and arrange repair
Discharge bilge water directly overboard at night, when the discharge cannot be seen
explanation: Bypassing the OWS is a serious offence.

question: Detergents and emulsifying cleaners should not be allowed to drain into the bilges because they:
options: Form stable emulsions that the OWS cannot separate properly
Improve the OWS performance by breaking up the oil droplets in the bilge water
Reduce bilge corrosion
Evaporate the oil
explanation: Use OWS-friendly cleaning products and keep chemicals out of the bilge system.

question: The standard discharge connection on deck is used to:
options: Take fresh water from shore
Connect the ship's sludge and oily bilge lines to shore hoses, using a standard flange
Discharge sewage overboard
Supply fuel to the ship from the bunker barge, using the flexible hose at the manifold
explanation: MARPOL Annex I gives the standard flange dimensions so any reception facility can connect.

question: Ships using separate fuels to comply with a SOx ECA must carry:
options: A scrubber manual only, because the fuel changeover is carried out automatically by the plant
A ballast water plan which shows the tanks used for storing the fuel during changeover
No documentation, as the changeover can be carried out as the officer on watch decides
A written fuel changeover procedure showing how the change is carried out
explanation: The procedure should allow enough time for the system to be fully flushed of high-sulphur fuel.

question: When entering a SOx ECA, the changeover to compliant fuel must be:
options: Fully completed before the ship enters the ECA
Done within 24 hours after entry
Done only in the next port
Started when the ship is inside the ECA, so that the engines run on the new fuel soon
explanation: When leaving the ECA, the changeover to higher-sulphur fuel should start only after exit.

question: MARPOL Annex VI NOx limits apply to marine diesel engines with a power output of more than:
options: 13 kW
130 kW
explanation: Engines used only for emergencies, such as emergency generators and lifeboat engines, are excluded.

question: Tier II NOx limits apply globally to diesel engines installed on ships constructed on or after:
options: 1 January 2020
1 January 1990
1 January 2000, the date from which Tier I limits applied to engines
1 January 2011
explanation: Tier I applies from 2000, and Tier III applies only in NOx ECAs.

question: An International Air Pollution Prevention (IAPP) Certificate is required for ships of:
options: 10,000 GT and above only
50 GT and above, including fishing vessels and small craft on coastal voyages
400 GT and above on international voyages
Passenger ships only
explanation: Its supplement records the ship's ODS systems, engines, fuel arrangements and incinerators.

question: Ships with rechargeable systems containing ozone-depleting substances must keep:
options: Only the Oil Record Book Part I, in which ODS recharges are entered as bunkering
A Garbage Record Book only, in which ODS refills are entered as operational waste
No record at all, since the amounts of refrigerant used on board are very small
An ODS record book, recording recharges, repairs, discharges and deliveries ashore
explanation: The ODS record book may also be part of an electronic record system.

question: Under MARPOL Annex VI, halon fire-extinguishing systems:
options: May be refilled and vented freely, provided the ship is outside port limits at the time
Are required for engine rooms on all ships, as the main fixed fire-fighting installation
May not be fitted as new installations, though existing ones may remain until replaced
Must be fitted on all new ships, as a condition of the fire protection rules of SOLAS
explanation: Halons have very high ozone depletion potential.

question: A closed-loop exhaust gas scrubber usually neutralises the sulphur with:
options: Urea
Fresh water dosed with caustic soda (sodium hydroxide)
Untreated sea water passed straight overboard, using the natural alkalinity of the water
Lubricating oil
explanation: Open-loop systems use the natural alkalinity of sea water instead.

question: 'Methane slip' in LNG-fuelled engines refers to:
options: Unburned methane escaping with the exhaust, which is a strong greenhouse gas
Loss of engine speed when the gas supply to the engine falls below its minimum pressure
Steam leaking from the boiler through the safety valve when the burner is on gas
Leaks of fuel oil from the pipes and joints of the fuel system into the engine room
explanation: Reducing methane slip is important to keep LNG's climate benefit.

question: A bunker delivery note must show, among other things:
options: The crew list of the barge and the name of the surveyor who sampled the fuel
The quantity, density and sulphur content of the fuel delivered
The ship's draught
The weather at the bunkering port
explanation: The supplier also declares that the fuel meets the relevant sulphur limit.

question: The MARPOL fuel sample should be taken:
options: At the ship's receiving manifold, by continuous drip throughout the delivery
From the barge's tank before delivery only, signed by the supplier's representative
From the engine's fuel filter after the fuel has been in use for some days
From the ship's tank after a week, once the fuel has settled and the water drained
explanation: The sample is sealed and signed by the supplier's representative and the ship's officer.

question: The Energy Efficiency Design Index (EEDI) applies to:
options: Only fishing vessels
Only ships in dry dock
Only ships older than 20 years, which have been converted to burn alternative fuels
New ships, setting a minimum design energy efficiency level
explanation: Required EEDI values have become stricter in phases since 2013.

question: To meet EEXI requirements, many existing ships have fitted:
options: Extra cargo tanks, in order to increase the carrying capacity and the transport work
Additional boilers to recover more heat from the exhaust gas and so reduce the fuel burned
Engine or shaft power limitation (EPL/ShaPoLi) that caps the available power
Larger main engines, to provide the extra power needed to meet the required EEXI value
explanation: The limit can be overridden only in emergencies, and such use must be recorded and reported.

question: Since October 2020, MARPOL allows the Oil Record Book to be kept:
options: Only on loose sheets of paper, with each page numbered and signed by the master
As an approved electronic record book
Only by the shore office
Only for ships under 400 GT
explanation: The electronic system must be approved by the Administration and keep entries secure from alteration.

question: If a ship's exhaust gas cleaning system breaks down, the ship should:
options: Continue burning high-sulphur fuel with no report, and note the failure in the log book only
Stop the main engine at sea for the rest of the voyage, until the system is repaired
Take corrective action, such as changing to compliant fuel, and inform the flag and port state
Discharge the scrubber washwater into the bilge, and take it ashore at the next port
explanation: IMO guidance and local rules describe what to do when an EGCS is not working.

question: SOx emissions from ships contribute mainly to:
options: Acid rain and fine particulate matter that harms human health
Increased ocean salinity
Ballast water invasive species
Ozone layer depletion, which is caused by halons and CFC refrigerants
explanation: This is why emission limits are strictest near populated coasts.

question: A SOPEP locker on deck typically contains:
options: Lifejackets and immersion suits for the clean-up team, with spare breathing apparatus
Fire hoses, nozzles and portable foam equipment for use on deck fires in port
Spare engine parts, tools and gaskets for the repair of the bunkering equipment
Absorbent materials, scoops, empty drums, plugs for scuppers and protective equipment
explanation: It is used to contain and clean up small spills on deck before oil reaches the sea.

question: In the Antarctic area, discharge of oil or oily mixtures from any ship is:
options: Prohibited
Allowed more than 50 miles from ice
Allowed below 15 ppm
Allowed only from the machinery space
explanation: The Antarctic area has the strictest MARPOL Annex I rules.

question: In Oil Record Book Part I, bunkering of fuel or bulk lubricating oil is recorded under code:
options: A, which is used for ballasting or cleaning of oil fuel tanks
D
H
C
explanation: Each entry uses a code letter and item number set out in the ORB instructions.

question: Which ORB Part I code is used to record the collection, transfer and disposal of oil residues (sludge)?
options: G
H, which is used for bunkering of fuel oil or bulk lubricating oil
A
C
explanation: Code D covers non-automatic discharge or disposal of bilge water.

question: Under the IMO performance standard for 15 ppm bilge alarms (MEPC.107(49)), the alarm must record date, time and alarm status, and keep the data for at least:
options: 10 years
18 months
24 hours, after which the data is overwritten by the next discharge
1 month
explanation: These records help inspectors verify OWS operation against the Oil Record Book.

question: A sludge tank on a ship built to current MARPOL requirements must have:
options: No discharge connection to the bilge system, the OWS or overboard, apart from approved drains
A connection to the fresh water system, so that the tank can be washed through with water
An open vent into the engine room, so that gases can escape through the casing
A direct overboard discharge valve with a locked handle, kept closed except in emergency
explanation: Sludge may only leave through the standard discharge connection or to an approved incinerator or boiler.

question: Under the MARPOL Annex VI amendments in force from 2022-2023, ships must have designated sampling points for:
options: Sewage effluent, so that it can be tested by port state control officers on arrival
Ballast water only, so that it can be tested by port state control officers
Boiler water, so that it can be tested for chlorides by the surveyors on board
The fuel oil in use, so that in-use samples can be taken and tested
explanation: Port state officers can then check whether the fuel being burned meets the sulphur limit.

question: If a ship cannot obtain compliant fuel despite its best efforts, MARPOL Annex VI expects the ship to:
options: Burn lubricating oil instead, mixed with the fuel to reduce the sulphur content
Submit a Fuel Oil Non-Availability Report (FONAR) to the flag state and destination port
Stop at sea until compliant fuel arrives, with the engines off and the ship drifting
Use any available fuel without telling anyone, and enter the grade used in the log book
explanation: The FONAR records the attempts made to buy compliant fuel; it does not automatically excuse non-compliance.

question: Each marine diesel engine certified under the NOx Technical Code must have on board:
options: Only the maker's sales brochure and the test bed certificate of the engine
A garbage management plan, which includes the handling of the used catalyst elements
An approved Technical File and, where used, a Record Book of Engine Parameters
The ship's stability booklet, since NOx control affects the trim of the vessel
explanation: Changes to NOx-critical components or settings must stay within the Technical File and be recorded.

question: MARPOL Annex VI NOx emission limits (in g/kWh) for each Tier depend on:
options: The engine's rated speed (rpm)
The sulphur content of the fuel
The number of cylinders only
The ship's gross tonnage
explanation: Slow-speed engines are allowed higher NOx in g/kWh than high-speed engines.

question: Under the IMO standard for shipboard incinerators, waste should not be fed in continuous operation until the combustion chamber flue gas outlet temperature reaches at least about:
explanation: High temperature ensures complete combustion and limits harmful emissions.

question: The washwater from an exhaust gas cleaning system must be monitored for:
options: Salinity only, since the discharge of sea water has no environmental effect
Sulphur content of the fuel
Oxygen content only
pH, PAH (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons) and turbidity
explanation: Some ports and coastal states also restrict or ban open-loop washwater discharge.

question: Inside an Annex I special area other than the Antarctic, machinery space bilge water may be discharged only if:
options: The master agrees and logs it, and the discharge is made outside the special area
It is processed through approved equipment to 15 ppm or less, with an automatic stop, en route
The ship is more than 3 nautical miles from land and the monitor is working normally
It is mixed with ballast water to dilute the oil content before it is discharged at sea
explanation: Oil-free water may also be discharged; all discharges must be recorded.

question: Since 1 July 2024, MARPOL Annex I has restricted the use and carriage as fuel of heavy fuel oil by ships operating in:
options: The Red Sea
The Caribbean Sea
Arctic waters
The Mediterranean Sea
explanation: Some ships may use waivers or exemptions until 2029; HFO has long been banned in the Antarctic area.
